chapters.title: Chapter 6: Markets at Work and in Your Pocket

lessons.title: Working at a Listed Company: Insider Trading Rules, Trading Windows and UPSI

children.text: If you work at a listed company, you are inside the regulatory perimeter whether or not anyone has explained it to you. Most insider trading cases involving employees do not feature a villain. They feature someone who genuinely did not know that the information on their screen was legally restricted. This lesson is the explanation you should have received on day one.

body.text: The rule does not ask whether you intended to cheat, or whether you made money. It asks whether you traded, or helped someone else trade, while in possession of information that was not yet public. Possession plus a trade is the offence.

children.text: The Three Words That Matter

markDefs.definition: Unpublished Price Sensitive Information: information relating to a company that is not generally available and which, once available, is likely to materially affect the price of its securities.
Under SEBI's insider trading regulations, a connected person or anyone in possession of or having access to UPSI. Employment is not required, and neither is seniority.
Employees and others identified by the company as covered by its internal code of conduct, typically subject to trading window restrictions, pre-clearance and disclosure requirements.

children.text: The regulations turn on
UPSI
, who counts as an
insider
, and which employees the company has named as
designated persons
. Note what is absent from those definitions: your grade, your function, and whether you actually understood the significance of what you saw.

body.caption: Is It UPSI? Some Working Examples

cells: Quarterly results already filed with the exchanges
Public information
Once filed and disseminated, it is generally available to everyone
The draft results deck you are formatting two days before the board meeting
UPSI
Not yet public, and clearly capable of moving the price
A large order win that has not yet been announced
Likely UPSI
Material and not generally available, even if the client has told your team
Acquisition discussions you overheard in a meeting room
Likely UPSI
Transactions of this kind are among the most sensitive categories
An imminent change in the CEO or CFO, not yet disclosed
Likely UPSI
Changes in key managerial personnel are treated as price sensitive
A newspaper report speculating about your company
Not UPSI by itself
Speculation in the public domain is not the same as inside information, though confirming it can be
Your own view that the stock looks cheap
Not UPSI
An opinion formed from public information is yours to act on, subject to your company's code

body.text: Seniority is irrelevant. An executive assistant scheduling an unusual board meeting, a designer building the results presentation, an IT administrator with access to the finance folder, and a plant supervisor who knows a major line has been shut all hold information that may be UPSI. The regulations reach the information, not the job title.

children.text: The Compliance Calendar You Live Inside

body.title: One Quarter, From a Designated Person's Point of View

events.title: The Trading Window Closes
events.description: Companies close the trading window for designated persons around the end of each quarter, because results are being compiled from that point onwards. You may not trade in company shares while it is shut.

events.title: Results Are Prepared
events.description: Numbers move through finance, audit and the board. Everyone touching them is in possession of UPSI, and the company records this in an internal database of who knew what and when.

events.title: Information Becomes Public
events.description: Results are filed with the exchanges and disseminated. Until that dissemination is complete, the information is still restricted.

events.title: The Window Reopens
events.description: Company codes typically reopen the window a prescribed period after results are made public, commonly 48 hours, giving the market time to absorb the information. Your compliance team publishes the exact reopening date.

events.title: Pre-Clearance, If Required
events.description: Above a threshold set in the company's code, designated persons must obtain written pre-clearance before transacting, and must then complete the trade within a specified number of days.

events.title: Disclosure and Contra-Trade Restrictions
events.description: Trades above a prescribed value must be disclosed to the company and onward to the exchanges, and reversing the transaction within a specified period, often six months, is typically prohibited.

body.text: Every number in that calendar, the reopening gap, the pre-clearance threshold, the contra-trade period and who counts as a designated person, comes from your own company's code of conduct, built on SEBI's regulations. The regulations set the floor and companies often go stricter. Read your code once; it is usually under ten pages and it is the document you would be judged against.

columns.label: You Must Not
points: Buy or sell your company's shares, directly or through anyone else
Pass the information to family, friends, brokers or advisers
Discuss it in places where it can be overheard, including group chats
Recommend that anyone buy or sell, even without stating your reason
Trade in a related listed company where the same information is material, such as a listed customer or target

columns.label: You May
points: Continue doing your job and sharing the information strictly on a need-to-know basis internally
Hold shares you already own without doing anything
Trade in unrelated companies, subject to your company's own code
Ask compliance before acting, which is always the cheapest step available
Continue your regular investments in diversified mutual funds, which your code will usually address explicitly

body.title: The Casual Question at Lunch
body.question: Results are three days away. A friend outside the company asks how the quarter went, and you reply, with no detail, that it looks like a good one. Your friend buys shares that afternoon. What is the position?
options: You are fine, because you gave no numbers
You are fine, because you did not trade yourself
This is potentially a serious problem, because passing on UPSI and enabling someone else to trade is itself prohibited
It only matters if your friend makes a profit
body.explanation: Communicating UPSI to someone who then trades is treated as a violation in its own right, and no numbers need to be shared for the substance of the information to be passed on. Whether your friend profited affects the penalty calculation, not whether a violation occurred. The safe answer to that question is that you cannot discuss unpublished results.

body.label: Why This Is Not a Technicality
body.context: The SEBI Act prescribes substantial monetary penalties for insider trading, running into crores or a multiple of the gain made, alongside the possibility of being barred from the securities market. Confirm the current provisions before quoting figures.

body.title: What HR Knows Before Anyone Else
body.scenario: You are a senior HR business partner at a listed company. You are working on a restructuring that will close one business unit and cut about 400 roles, to be announced along with results in three weeks. Your spouse holds shares in your employer in their own demat account, bought years ago, and mentions over dinner that they are thinking of selling to fund a house renovation.
body.prompt: What do you do, and what must you not do?
body.modelAnswer: Treat the restructuring as UPSI, because it is unpublished and plainly capable of moving the price. Two things follow immediately. First, you must not tell your spouse anything about it, including hints, a general suggestion to wait, or advice to sell now. Second, and this is the part people get wrong, the trade itself is the problem regardless of what you say, because immediate relatives are typically covered by the regulations and your company's code, and a sale by your spouse while you hold UPSI can be attributed to you. The practical course is to go to compliance today, before anything happens, and say exactly this: you hold UPSI, your spouse independently wishes to sell, and you need guidance. Companies deal with this situation regularly and have a process for it. What you must not do is decide the answer yourself, tell your spouse to go ahead because the sale was their idea, or quietly hope nobody connects the two accounts, since exchange surveillance and the company's own insider database are designed precisely to connect them. Expect the likely outcome to be that the sale waits until after the announcement and the window reopens, which is inconvenient but survivable, and note that documenting your disclosure to compliance protects you far more than silence does. Separately, apply the same discipline to the restructuring itself: share it internally strictly on a need-to-know basis, keep drafts off personal devices and group chats, and remember that the 400 people affected also have a right not to learn about their jobs through a leak.

body.title: How Companies and Exchanges Actually Catch This

children.text: Enforcement is far more systematic than most employees assume:
The insider database.

Listed companies are required to maintain a structured record of who was given UPSI, what it related to and when. If an investigation starts, that record is the first document requested, and it is designed to be tamper-evident.
Exchange surveillance.
Exchanges run automated systems that flag unusual volume and price activity ahead of announcements, then work backwards through the trading records to find who transacted.
Linked accounts.

PAN-linked records make it straightforward to connect an employee to trades in the accounts of family members and associates. Using someone else's account is not a workaround, it is an aggravating factor.
Communication trails.
Investigations examine messages, call records and emails. Several Indian cases have turned on messages sent in group chats by people who assumed the conversation was private.
The practical implication is that the question is never whether a trade can be traced. It can. The question is only whether there is an innocent explanation available when it is.
The ESOP Question Everyone Asks

Employees with vested options routinely ask whether a closed trading window blocks them. The honest general answer is that exercising options and selling the resulting shares are treated as two different acts, and company codes commonly handle them differently. Because the treatment varies and the rules have been amended more than once, this is a question for your compliance team in writing, not for a colleague's recollection. Ask early, because vesting and exercise deadlines do not pause for a window closure.

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: Information about a listed company that is not generally available and is likely to materially affect its share price once published is called ___.
body.explanation: UPSI stands for unpublished price sensitive information. The two tests are that it is not generally available and that it is likely to be material to the price. Both must hold.

body.title: Your Personal Compliance Routine
steps: Find out whether you are a designated person under your company's code, and ask in writing if you are unsure
Read the code of conduct once, particularly the sections on the trading window, pre-clearance and immediate relatives
Note who your compliance officer is and how to reach them before you need to
Assume any unpublished number, deal, appointment or restructuring you see at work is restricted until it is on the exchange website
Keep work information off personal devices and out of group chats, including family ones
Tell your immediate family that their trades in your employer's shares can become your problem
When in doubt, ask compliance and keep the reply, because a documented approval is the cheapest protection you will ever get

cards.definition: Unpublished price sensitive information: not generally available, and likely to materially affect the share price once published.
A connected person, or anyone in possession of or with access to UPSI. Seniority and intent are irrelevant.
An employee or other person identified by the company as subject to its insider trading code.
The period during which designated persons may transact in company shares. It is closed around results and other sensitive events.
Written approval required from the compliance officer before transacting above a threshold set in the company's code.
Reversing a transaction within a restricted period after it, which company codes typically prohibit.
Defined family members whose trades can be attributed to an insider, which is why family accounts are covered.
The principle that UPSI is shared only with those who require it for a legitimate purpose, and no one else.
The internal record listed companies maintain of who received UPSI, what it concerned and when.

body.label: SEBI: Insider Trading Regulations
body.description: The prohibition of insider trading regulations, along with amendments and FAQs, are published on SEBI's website. Read them alongside your own company's code of conduct, since the code is what you are directly bound by.

points: Insider trading turns on possession of unpublished price sensitive information at the time of a trade, not on intent, seniority or profit
UPSI has two tests: it is not generally available, and it is likely to be material to the share price
Passing information to someone who then trades is a violation in itself, even without numbers or an explicit recommendation
Trading windows close around results and reopen a prescribed period after they are made public, with the exact dates published by your compliance team
Pre-clearance, disclosure and contra-trade restrictions apply to designated persons above thresholds set in the company's own code
Immediate relatives are covered, so a family member's trade can become your regulatory problem
Exercising options and selling the resulting shares are treated differently, and that question belongs to compliance in writing
Enforcement is systematic: insider databases, exchange surveillance, PAN-linked accounts and message trails all connect trades to people

body.text: This lesson is educational and is not legal, compliance or investment advice. Insider trading law in India is governed by the SEBI Act and SEBI's prohibition of insider trading regulations, which have been amended several times, including the definitions of UPSI, the treatment of trading plans and the obligations of designated persons. Thresholds, periods and categories described here are typical rather than definitive. Your obligations come from your own company's code of conduct and the regulations as they currently stand, so consult your compliance officer or a qualified professional before acting.
